title: Void Ending in a Sextile to Uranus
source: Picatrix (adapted), Book I chapter 5, Book II chapter 3 and Book III chapter 1

<!-- generated by tools/content/gen-void.ts; edit the generator, not this file -->

The sextile is one of the two friendly aspects. Picatrix ties the Moon to the fortunes by trine and sextile whenever a work is meant to prosper, and grades the sextile as the aspect of moderate friendship: the signs it joins are kin in action but not in passion, so the concord between them is a lukewarm one.

When the Moon closes her course in a sign with a sextile to Uranus, the quiet stretch that follows carries something of his cold, sky-borne surprises. Uranus is nowhere in Picatrix: the planet was found with a telescope in 1781, some seven centuries after the book was written, and no passage of the source speaks of it. What follows is this almanac's extension of Picatrix's doctrine, never the medieval text's own words. Named for the Greek god of the sky, it is read here as a cold, far, sky-colored planet of upheaval, so that a course closing on it ends on a surprise rather than a settled end.
